grammar.note_en:
Read the first-use meanings before the story. The new forms are whole forms to learn, not a rule that adds ています directly to a ます ending. Earlier request forms help: はこんで → はこんでいます, よんで → よんでいます. This chapter additionally teaches もって / もっています, “hold / is holding.” Story requests with もってください mean “please hold.”

Actions in progress include あめがふっています (“rain is falling”), かぜがふいています (“wind is blowing”), みずがはいっています (“water is coming in”), and みずがおちています (“water is falling”). These four weather/water が frames identify a phenomenon occurring; they do not introduce arbitrary contrastive human-agent が. In this chapter, people remain topics with は. はこんでいます means “is carrying”; ひろげています, “is spreading out”; よんでいます, “is reading”; みています, “is looking”; おさえています, “is pressing/supporting”; いれています, “is putting/pouring in.”

For these verbs describing a change whose result continues, the same polite shape describes a present result: あいています “is open,” ぬれています “is wet,” and やぶれています “is torn.” The wrapping first tears (やぶれます); afterwards it is torn (やぶれています). A page can remain wet after the rain stops. Do not read all ています forms as an English progressive action. We do not generalise every Japanese verb to a result meaning.

The polite negative replaces います with いません: みていません “is not looking,” ぬれていません “is not wet,” ふっていません “rain is not falling.” These are verb forms, not a new adjective-negative paradigm. まだ means “still” here, with a continuing positive action/state. A not-yet construction is not introduced. おちました reuses the known polite verb past to report a leaf that fell. No plain ている, plain relative clause, adjective past, potential or ていました is taught here.

The tables list complete attested expressions; the quick reference below pairs each with its English meaning. All new inflections are dated to this chapter, including the previously unintroduced wet/torn/open result forms. The seven new characters occur in familiar whole words: まち, みち, かわ, えき, ちず, まど. The two previously seen characters in てがみ also support whole familiar かみ and て here; their new whole-word written forms are dated separately. せん is a drawn line in this story, a separate meaning from the money word for one thousand. みかんせい is a noun: みかんせいです means “it is unfinished,” and みかんせいのちず means “an unfinished map.”

In the map description, かわまでです means “as far as the river”: まで marks the route’s endpoint. えきへのせん means “a line towards the station”; direction へ joins the following noun with の. In the rescue, ページのしたにてをいれます means “put a hand under the page,” using に for the receiving position. The new tearing verb names a change in the wrapper: つつみのしたがやぶれます means “the bottom of the wrapping tears.”

Quick reference — Japanese and English pairs

Ongoing actions — Japanese expression and English meaning

ふっています — Rain is falling.

ふっていません — Rain is not falling.

もっています — is holding

はこんでいます — is carrying

ひろげています — is spreading out

よんでいます — is reading

みていません — is not looking

いれています — is putting/pouring in

Present results — Japanese expression and English meaning

あいています — is open (the window)

ぬれています — is wet (the page or wrapping)

ぬれていません — is not wet

やぶれています — is torn (the wrapping)

まだぬれています — is still wet

Change and present result — complete examples

つつみのしたが、やぶれます。 — The bottom of the wrapping tears.

つつみのしたが、やぶれています。 — The bottom of the wrapping is torn.

ページは、したからおちました。 — The page fell from below.
